en: Preface to the *Heart Sūtra* Commentary on Carving the Wheel:

In the first year of the Taichang era, while I was observing the winter retreat at Yunmen, it was snowing and raining. Amidst this solitude, I gathered with two or three dharma friends to discuss the Way;
when we reached the various sūtras, we would invariably expound upon them, yet there was one kind we had never yet treated: the *Heart Sūtra*.
"If these words were to be used on another day by one serving as a presiding master for devas and humans, it would be improper to depart from this matter in mere silence.
Thereupon, I took up my brush and completed the commentary within ten days.

In the spring of the following year, the *Xinyou* year of the Tianqi era, having heard that Master Yiyu was expounding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, I respectfully presented this interpretation to him to seek correction.
When Master An-shi first read through the scroll and took it with him, Cheng Yun composed a preface for it.

Subsequently, our exchanges within the lecture hall became frequent and manifold, yet the agreement we made was not fulfilled; since we have had no prospect of meeting again, seven years have already passed unnoticed.
This commentary, retrieved from my bag, has likewise become a thing of the past. Nevertheless, that which was written in the past remains [the same] as that which is now...
To observe existence is like seeing the omens of a bad harvest during a year of plenty; it is sufficient to realize that [the views] can be reduced to ashes.

Now, we hear that five hundred bhikṣus each interpreted the Buddha’s words differently and asked, "Who among you accords with the Buddha's intent? The Buddha said, "None of these accord with my intent.

The assembly said, "If none accord with the Buddha's intent, will we not incur offense? The Buddha said, "Although they do not accord with my intent, each follows correct principle and is fit to serve as the holy teaching."
If one considers that there is merit in this and no fault, then the old interpretations may be preserved while new insights are introduced;
it is permissible to record them hereafter to clarify that both [approaches] are indeed commentaries on the Buddha’s words.

Furthermore, regarding the intent behind annotating the scriptures, some desire to follow what is vast and extensive for the sake of delighting in much learning, while others desire to follow what is concise and abbreviated; yet there is also a desire to follow both perspectives.
Because those who have attained what they take as their primary tenet are often biased, in the lecture halls and in exegesis, one must strive for an open mind;

one must not hold this to be right while condemning that as wrong. Thus it is said: "What is loathed is the adherence to a single [view], for it robs the Way of its integrity, taking up one thing and abandoning a hundred others.

Nevertheless, although commentaries on the *Heart Sūtra* are so numerous that they could exhaust oxen with sweat and fill the rafters of houses, there is only one that possesses the resonance of metal and the purity of jade—and that is my own.
This commentary shall not be further scrutinized for its measure; it is here recorded simply because the lay devotee Cai Fuyan requested its publication to mark the date.
Thus concludes the "Carving the Wheel" Commentary on the Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom by Biefeng Tongrong.
Expounded by the later-generation monk Feiyin Tongrong of Fuzhou.
*Prajñā* in Sanskrit means "wisdom"; *pāramitā* in Sanskrit means "reaching the other shore.

While the meaning of "reaching the other shore" (*pāramitā*) emphasizes the attainment of the ultimate goal, the meaning of "wisdom" (*prajñā*) is considered somewhat secondary. Here, we follow [the former].

Because "respect" (zunzhong) is not subject to translation, the Sanskrit term is retained to establish the name. Furthermore, the meaning of *prajñā* (wisdom) comprises five aspects: first, the wisdom of ultimate reality (*dharmatā-prajñā*);
second, the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*); third, the wisdom of words (*vyañjana-prajñā*); fourth, the wisdom of the objective sphere (*viṣaya-prajñā*);

and fifth, the wisdom of its retinue (*parivāra-prajñā*). Regarding what is called the wisdom of ultimate reality: it refers to the principle realized, which is fundamentally and originally true. When...
The *dharmatā-prajñā* (wisdom of the true nature) is the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) by which one realizes the emptiness of all phenomena through the knowing intellect that can realize it;

thus, being free from further obstructions, one suddenly accords with the source of the mind. The *vyañjana-prajñā* (wisdom of words) refers to the essence of the teaching that expresses [the truth], which accords with principle without omission;
it is not merely a mundane tool of unfeeling letters. As for the *ālambana-prajñā* (wisdom of the objective sphere), it is by means of...
Regarding objective conditions, there is ultimately nothing good or bad; thus, one does not give rise to hatred or love, remaining ever lucid and as-it-is.
Those who take Prajñā as their kin govern all phenomena through principle and spirit, wondrously harmonizing with the midst of the universe.
Neither contradicting nor opposing, they unify everything into a single principle. Now, observing this sutra, it truly encompasses five aspects; for the principle realized therein is true emptiness.

Not a single dharma exists; for instance, the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six sense bases (*āyatana*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the four noble truths (*satya*), the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the six perfections (*pāramitā*)—all these dharmas are entirely empty in their very substance. Their original essence is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which is precisely the *prajñāpāramitā* of the true mark.
As it says: "When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara was practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, he clearly perceived the five aggregates..."

This "equality" is precisely the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*). Because it can, in a single thought-moment, illuminate the root-source of all phenomena and instantaneously enter the state of non-arising, it is the wisdom of contemplation.
From the Buddha down to the bodhisattvas, there is a divine communion of subject and object;

they observe the faculties [of beings] to provide appropriate teachings and expound meanings according to the occasion. Within the words of this single sutra, whether read vertically or horizontally, great benefit is produced—this is not of the mundane world.
The vessel of insentience is precisely the *prajñā* of words (*vāk-prajñā*). As in the subsequent passage: "Because the Bodhisattva relies on *prajñā*, his mind is without hindrance;
he is without fear; he is far removed from perverted thoughts and dreams; he attains ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
This refers to the four truths alone and the absence of the four inversions, which is the *prajñā* of the objective realm (*viṣaya-prajñā*). As in the subsequent passage regarding *prajñā*...

If it is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra, an unsurpassed mantra, and an unequaled mantra, then one knows that the wondrous resonance of Prajñā with the three virtues is like a ring without end; this is the *prajñā* of the retinue.

Although the meaning is explained here first, it manifests later; yet Prajñā is ultimately one, and these five meanings arise according to its various functions. These functions correspond to the five meanings.

On the "this shore" (the mundane), one establishes the "other shore" (nirvana). If one does not clearly understand *prajñā*, then ignorance (*avidyā*), delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*), the habitual tendencies of names and words (*nāma-pada-vāsanā*), fear, and inversion—in short, the entanglements of the three delusions—are all the karma of birth and death.

Looking toward that which is beyond birth and death, it is called the "this shore. Once *prajñā* is clearly understood, ignorance is then no longer ignorance, and delusive conceptualization is then no longer [delusive conceptualization].
Delusory thoughts and names are themselves not names; terror is itself not terror.

To speak in general terms, when illusions are extinguished and completely exhausted, the light of wisdom becomes perfectly round and complete. This is what is meant by "when birth and death have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests. In relation to all arising and ceasing, this is called the "other shore.
Upon reaching this, it cannot be named, nor can it be described; it cannot be grasped even by following the paths of the teachings.
That which is circulated throughout the world as the standard is called "mind. The subtlety of this mind is unknowable, and even knowing it is difficult to discern;
its realization is granted only to those who enter through awakening. If one awakens to this mind, then body and mind are as one, and there is nothing remaining outside of the mind.

Only then will one know that all the teachings of the Tathāgata throughout his lifetime, including the hundreds of thousands of samādhis and immeasurable wondrous gateways, are [all contained herein].
The extent of this mind reaches even to ordinary people of the mundane world who manage their livelihoods, engage in labor, and perform their tasks;
whether seeing forms or hearing sounds, there is nothing that is not this very message—it is simply that they lack the power of awakening (*bodhi*).
Therefore it is said: "This mind alone permits entry through awakening; the sūtra is the Way. This is because the Dharma of the mind is what is expounded by this sūtra.

Because it allows one to enter the Great Way, and because "sūtra" (經) means "constant," this sūtra expounds the mental dharmas as the eternal law that remains unchanged through antiquity and the present.

According to the fivefold profound meaning (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*), this sūtra takes a single dharma as its name, true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) as its essence, contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*) as its school (*śāstra*), the crossing over suffering as its function, and the "ripened butter" of the Mahāyāna as its doctrinal characteristic. [O] Formerly...
While Duke Huan was reading in the hall above, Lun Pian was planing wheels in the hall below.
Setting aside his mallet and chisel, he ascended and addressed Duke Huan, saying, "May I venture to ask what it is you are reading? The Duke said, "The words of the sages.

Lun Pian said, "Are the sages still present? The Duke said, "They have already passed away. Lun Pian said, "If that is so, then what you are reading— "Please provide the remainder of the text for a complete translation."
"Reader, you have merely consumed the dregs and lees of the ancients! Duke Huan said, "I am a man of books; how can a wheelwright presume to criticize me?
If you have a reason, it may be accepted; if not, you shall die. Wheelwright Bian replied, "Your servant observes his own work:
when I hew a wheel too slowly, it feels easy but is not firm; when I do so too quickly, it is difficult and the tool does not enter the wood. It is neither slow nor fast."
"It is not that one can quickly acquire it with the hand and respond to it with the mind;
there is something that cannot be expressed in words, for a certain principle exists between them. I am unable to explain it to my son, nor can my son receive it from me.
Therefore, at seventy years of age, I have grown old at this wheelwright's craft. The ancients had things that could not be transmitted."
Such a person is dead; thus, what you have been reading is but the dregs and husks of the ancients.

As for the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, "observation" (guan) has two meanings: first, the observing wisdom (guan-hui); second, the true reality (shi-xiang) that is observed. When the observer and the observed are in accord, [this is true observation].
Realizing this name is "sovereignty" (vaśitā); by using the principle of this realization to guide sentient beings, one is called a Bodhisattva.

Because all sentient beings fail to turn back from their deluded cognitions, they give rise to the three poisons and create various karmas, cycling through the three realms, rising and falling, ascending and descending, for kalpas beyond measure, without anyone attaining sovereignty. Only this Bodhisattva understands [this].
All phenomena are the realm of emptiness; wisdom is suchness. Abiding in birth and death, one is not bound by the roots of birth and death;

abiding in nirvana, one is not fettered by the fruits of nirvana. Even the realm of ordinary beings is suchness, the realm of śrāvakas is suchness, the realm of non-Buddhists is suchness, the realm of the Māra kings is suchness;
this world is suchness, other worlds are suchness—such is the true Great Lion King.

Fearlessness is mastery. However, according to the general principle of this teaching, if within one's own sphere there is nothing that engages the mind—neither projecting outward nor drawing inward—and the body and mind are like walls, then one enters the unborn (*anutpāda*).
Thus, one’s entire body and eyes become pervasive; what root of birth and death could there be to bind one, and what obstacle of right and wrong could there be to hinder?
Thus, one who is able to suddenly awaken to their own mind and take full responsibility for it is named Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
When practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*,...
The "practitioner" is the wisdom that is able to enter into accord; "profound *prajñā*" is the principle of wisdom into which one enters;
"time" is the moment when both subject and object are forgotten and both wisdom and principle are extinguished.
Yet, why is this *prajñā* called "profound"? It is because this *prajñā* is formless, signless, directionless, placeless, and without interior or exterior.
Externally there is no limit; if one seeks the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), it is not found in that which has marks (*sanimitta*), for where there are marks, there is nothingness.

If one seeks it in that which is markless (*animitta*), it is not found in that which lacks marks, for where there are no marks, there is nothingness. In truth, it is like a spark from a flint or a flash of lightning—there is no room for deliberation.

One must attain a depth that is deeper than deep, yet "depth" is still a mark; one must achieve a penetration that is more penetrating than penetrating, yet "penetration" is still a name. Only by being neither name nor mark can one bring [it] forth.
The icchantikas, being of evil nature, view it as a great mass of fire, unable to approach from any of the four sides;
yet it enables the true sons of the Mahāyāna to view it as a cool pond, through which all four gates may be entered.

Thus we know that the merit of Prajñā is great and powerful, and there is indeed a reason for its being named "profound. Furthermore, there are five points of correspondence regarding Prajñā: first, [the correspondence with]... (text continues).
That is to say, the five seals are identical to the one seal, just as a ring has no beginning or end; how could there be any deviation from this principle?

Thus, practice is identical to profound *prajñā*, and profound *prajñā* is identical to practice; truly, in a single thought, at a single moment, and within a single limit, one enters suddenly into the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
This is as explained in the eighth section on the Dharma-gates of the Five Stages in the *Dazhuangyanjing lun* (Treatise on the Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Adornment of the Great Vehicle).
The realization of the Way occurs in a single moment, a single juncture, a single *kṣaṇa*, allowing no second thought or second instant;

there is no distance or proximity between them. It is like the Zen school’s teaching that to deliberate is ten thousand miles of white clouds, and to conceptualize is a ghost cave amidst black mountains.
One reaches the point where opening one's mouth creates a pair of pegs, and silence falls into two or three parts—only through silent resonance can one truly understand.
This may be called practicing profound prajñā.
"To perceive that the five aggregates are all empty, and thus transcend all suffering and calamity.
This explains how it was previously stated that this bodhisattva enters into the extremely profound prajñā—by what means is this achieved?

The commentary states: This Bodhisattva, from the very beginning, is able through the power of contemplative insight to penetrate and perceive, within a single thought-moment, the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (skandhas)—also called the five *āyatanas*.
The "aggregate" (*skandha*) refers to the accumulation of karmic formations; the "aggregate" (*āyatana*) refers to the veil of the true principle.
Because of these karmic formations and the veiling of the true principle, hearing does not transcend sound and seeing does not go beyond form.
To enter the cycle of saṃsāra through form is a great harm. Furthermore, within these five aggregates, there is at this very moment a fivefold aggregate of real fruits;

yet now, by clearly seeing that "the five aggregates are all empty," one thoroughly perceives that within a single thought-moment the five aggregates are utterly and completely void, and the life-faculty is severed.
This is because, within a single thought-moment, the realization of the principle is firm and stable.
To experience this principle is called the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha); to contemplate this principle is called the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha);
to undergo the transformation of this principle is called the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha); and to discern this principle is called the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha).
Although these five aggregates are spoken of sequentially, in reality they exist within a single moment during the practitioner’s engagement with the twelve sense bases.
The effort of selection and rejection does not depart from this mindfulness; if one departs from this mindfulness, it is what the Chan school calls severing the life-root (*jīvitendriya*).
If the life-root is severed, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of the karmic fruit naturally attain liberation. As the saying goes:
"If the skin no longer exists, where can the hair remain? Now, this Bodhisattva, having first grasped [the essence], proceeds without looking back.
Subsequently, regarding gain and loss, right and wrong, or acceptance and rejection, it is like grasping a single-edged vajra sword to sever a single strand of silk;
there is no longer any distinction between what is severed and what is not. This is truly called the sudden realization of true emptiness and the entry into the state of non-arising.
If this is so, what karmic retribution would not be penetrated, and what suffering or calamity would not be transcended? Therefore, it is said: "To deliver."
I say that all suffering and calamity refers to the actual fruit of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which is explained in detail below.

Since there are actual fruits of the five aggregates, there must necessarily be the retributive suffering of the three realms. Although this retributive suffering is manifold, it does not exceed the eight types of suffering.
These eight sufferings are truly perilous and distressing—just as Xuan Sha said: "It is like the moon's reflection in a cold pond; it is still."
The sound of the night bell follows each strike without fail; it touches the waves without dispersing.
This is still merely a matter on the shore of birth and death. One must know that as long as one remains here, one still belongs to the realm of birth and death;

thus, these lingering thoughts of acceptance and rejection—what are they other than the five aggregates? Only those of extraordinary capacity, such as Deshan and Linji, do not fall within this category.
It is limited.
Śāriputra, form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form; form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form.
In the Sanskrit language, "Śāri" means "partridge," and this Venerable One’s mother had eyes as sharp as those of a partridge.
The people of that time borrowed this name to praise him; because the Venerable One derived his name from his mother, he was called Śāriputra.

Among the assembly of śrāvakas, this Venerable One was foremost in wisdom. Because his wisdom was capable of entering into Prajñāpāramitā, the World-Honored One specifically summoned and addressed him.
This is because śrāvakas do not realize that the solid and substantial aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is like an illusion.

Those who do not grasp reality seek to analyze form (*rūpa*) to clarify emptiness (*śūnyatā*), engaging in various acts of selection and rejection to cultivate diverse contemplations of weary detachment.
They view the three realms as a prison and the physical body as shackles;
thus, in the Deer Park, many have abandoned their bodies like discarded brooms, driven by necessity to enter the forest and destroy them. At that time, the World-Honored One did not [permit this].
I dared to explain to him that the myriad dharmas are fundamentally empty;
however, fearing that my disciples might suddenly become terrified and lose their resolve, I gradually refined and tested them over many years.

Now, having reached this assembly of the Prajñāpāramitā, their faculties are quite mature and they have come to trust me; therefore, I dare to call out and announce this before the multitude of devas and humans.
I say this because you, as a śrāvaka, do not know that all phenomena are fundamentally empty; you practice in vain, realize in vain, and grasp at nirvāṇa in vain.
You simply do not understand that such vain practice and vain realization are inconsistent with the principle of true emptiness.
Furthermore, observe this bodhisattva practicing profound prajñā—what hardship has he ever undergone? How peaceful!

By eliminating [delusions] and attaining that alone, one single thought-moment penetrates the realization that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are, in their very essence, entirely empty, and one is thereby liberated.
Since this is so, you should reflect and awaken to the fact that you must know all phenomena arise from conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna*) and fundamentally lack any substantial reality.
You do not realize this, and thus you falsely assume that this solid physical body is something accumulated that differs from the true emptiness; in fact, it is not so.
One might mistakenly think that emptiness is distinct from form, or that emptiness differs from material substance; yet in reality, emptiness is not distinct from form. Why is this?
It is because both this form and emptiness arise from conditions. Since both arise from conditions, how could form and emptiness be different?
Therefore it is said: "Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. Thus, as for form...
Since both emptiness and form arise from conditions, emptiness gives rise to form; these two types exist within my own mind as nothing more than names and appearances, devoid of substantial reality.
Thus, the title *Heart Sūtra* possesses profound significance.
Furthermore, since both form and emptiness arise from conditions, the nature of form and emptiness is non-dual. Since their nature is non-dual, one need not seek it outside of form.
Beyond the emptiness of emptiness, one becomes weary of form; yet because this emptiness is form and this form is emptiness, it is said that "form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form.
However, there is no need to rejoice in the realm beyond as Nirvana, nor to loathe the realm within as a prison.
Right here, within this very aggregate of form resulting from karmic retribution, there is complete and total liberation. Why labor to analyze and dismantle form before [attaining it]?

"It is so. If one asks about the difference between 'it' and 'that,' how would one distinguish them? I say: those who do not speak of their non-difference are like those who do not recognize the light of a lamp;
they will claim that the lamp is not the light, or that the light is not the lamp. If someone were to point it out for them, saying, 'The lamp is not different from the light;
the light is not different from the lamp,' only then would they realize that the lamp has always been the light."

The original meaning is that this is precisely the lamp; one must know that the words "not different" initiate the beginning of principle, while the words "precisely this" meet the source of principle.
Having finished the analysis of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) above, the following analyzes the other four aggregates.

This is because ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*) are still heavily attached to the solid self-clinging regarding this aggregate of form; thus they cling to houses, wealth, property, and even down to a single [unit].
Those who speak of physical contact and harbor resentment until the end of their lives are likewise beyond counting;
this is truly due to the fault of stubborn attachment to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). [The interlocutor] asked: "Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom;

could he also be like this? [The Buddha] replied: "I addressed Śāriputra in order to admonish ordinary people. [The interlocutor] asked: "If that is so, why not address ordinary people directly instead of addressing you?"
The Bodhisattva said: "If you were to speak to an ordinary person, that ordinary person is already deluded; how could they understand immediately?
If you were to speak to a Bodhisattva, that Bodhisattva has already realized it. Now, if you suddenly speak to them, they will surely give rise to doubt.

This is because the World-Honored One, in the assembly of the Vaipulya sutras, praised and extolled the Bodhisattvas while rebuking the Śrāvakas. If he were to speak [to us] now, would not doubt arise?"

For these two reasons, he did not inform them; he informed only the śrāvakas because the śrāvakas were already at a high level where there was still the stage of a bodhisattva for them to ascend to, whereas those below had easily transcended the category of ordinary beings and were already fully enlightened.
Furthermore, ordinary people would have felt such profound yearning that they would have thought: "If even Śāriputra has not yet attained full realization, how much less [can others]?"
I do not exert myself [regarding this].
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise thus.
By this, one may infer by analogy that the preceding aggregate of form is also dependently originated. As for what is called "feeling":
Its nature is that of experiencing, because it experiences the three types of objects—those that are agreeable, disagreeable, and neither. Its function is to give rise to craving:
toward agreeable objects, it gives rise to craving for union; toward disagreeable objects, it gives rise to craving for separation;

and toward objects that are neither, which have not yet been reached, it gives rise to craving for non-separation, while toward those already reached, it gives rise to craving for non-union. However, as for this nature...

All karma lacks substantial reality; if it possessed substantial reality, then when experiencing a favorable condition, it would ultimately possess a favorable nature, and upon encountering an adverse object, it would logically not arise [as such].
How then could hatred arise upon encountering an adverse object?

Since this is the case for both the adverse and the favorable, and neither can be reversed, we know that these three objects lack mutual substantiality. Since they lack substantiality, they are not empty.
How is it that one knows sensation (*vedanā*) is itself emptiness (*śūnyatā*), yet is able to experience the three objects?

It is not sensation. How is it that one knows emptiness is itself sensation? Thus, emptiness is not empty of itself; it is empty because of sensation. Sensation is not sensation of itself; it is sensation because of emptiness.
One thereby knows that these two—emptiness and sensation—arise mutually through conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna*), and these conditions are themselves... [self-empty].
This is the wondrous responsiveness of the mind. Nevertheless, if one examines this aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), it is also termed a "characteristic" (*nimitta*);

how then could it exist apart from one's own mind? As for what is called the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), its nature consists in grasping the images of objects, and its function is the establishment of various names and conventions.
It is only by establishing distinctions upon objects that one can subsequently give rise to various names and conventions.

However, this nature of mental activity (*citta-karma*) also lacks substantial reality. If one perceives a preceding object, and that object possesses substantial reality, one would no longer perceive a subsequent object;

yet since one does indeed perceive a subsequent object, it is known that the former lacks substantial reality. If there is no substantial reality, what is it other than emptiness? Thus, one knows that perception itself is emptiness.

Furthermore, the ability to form mental images follows the application of conventional designations (*prajñapti*); if it were not perception, how could such things exist? Thus, one knows that emptiness is perception.

That is to say, perception (*saṃjñā*) is likewise empty; it does not become empty of itself, but is empty because of perception, while perception does not perceive of itself, but perceives because of emptiness.

Thus one knows that emptiness and perception are mutually dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). By inferring this, even that which is called "characteristic" (*nimitta*) within one's own mind is [subject to this].
As for what is called the "aggregate of formations" (*saṃskāraskandha*), its meaning is flux and volitional activity; it is momentary and impermanent, arising and ceasing from moment to moment.
The transition of death and birth, and birth and death, is like a whirling firebrand, never pausing for a moment. Yet even this has no real nature;
if that nature were internal, it should not transition to the external, and if it were external, it should not transition to the internal.

Knowing thus that neither the internal nor the external can be apprehended—how could it be anything other than emptiness? Know further that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is itself emptiness, yet it can also blaze forth and undergo transition.

If transformation is not the formations (*saṃskāra*), what then is it? This shows that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is itself the aggregate of formations. Thus, emptiness and formations likewise arise from conditions;

they are the names and characteristics of emptiness and formations within our own minds. As for what is called the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), there are three types of consciousness:

first, the *ālaya*; second, the *manas*; and third, the consciousness that cognizes objects. Furthermore, regarding the consciousness that cognizes objects, it may also be termed "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).

From consciousness up to the consciousness of phenomena (*dharmavijñāna*), names are established according to their respective objects in accordance with the nature of consciousness; that is to say, the discernment of the six objects is called "consciousness.

Furthermore, these three types of consciousness are fundamentally empty in nature, arising and ceasing in mutual dependence like the stalks of a *naḍa* reed-bundle, such that they are ultimately ungraspable.
Since they are ungraspable, what are they other than emptiness? Thus, one knows that the aggregate of consciousness is itself emptiness, and furthermore—

If one discerns various objects, what could it be other than consciousness? Thus, one knows that emptiness is precisely consciousness. Observing it in this way, both emptiness and consciousness arise from conditions;
within my own mind, they are fundamentally like dreams and illusions. Emptiness and consciousness are merely names and appearances.

In sum, the four aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are themselves true emptiness, and true emptiness is itself these four; therefore, feeling, perception, and so forth... [are likewise empty].
The consciousness of formations is likewise so. My intention is that Śāriputra must know the five aggregates are thus illusory;
why labor over them to vainly eliminate the aggregates? Question: If one cannot realize that the nature of dependent origination is emptiness, by what skillful means can one guide such a person?
Answer: Simply observe: before your parents were born, where was this body?

Abiding in this established state, do not permit yourself to speculate, calculate, or provide intellectual explanations; keep this in mind with focused mindfulness, and after a long time, you will naturally lose your nose.
Śāriputra, the mark of the emptiness of all phenomena is that they are neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.

Having previously traced the emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha*) and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as being without intrinsic substance, one must now realize that these ultimately converge within one’s own mind;
thus, this sutra takes the mind as its primary subject. For when the preceding emptiness of the aggregates is contrasted with them, one knows that the aggregates belong to dependent origination;

since the aggregates belong to dependent origination, one knows that emptiness is not external to the aggregates. Since emptiness is not external to the aggregates, this true emptiness likewise arises from conditions. This is the point.
Within this mind of one's own, the dharmas of the aggregates (*skandha*) cannot be apprehended, nor can the dharma of ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) be apprehended.
For ultimate emptiness is but a name and a mark (*nāma-rūpa*), and the dharmas of the aggregates are likewise name and mark.
Since these two belong to the category of name and mark, they are fundamentally unapprehendable within one's own mind. Therefore, it is said: "This..."
If the empty nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*) is thus, how could it not be the realization of the mind? Question: Does this mind not follow conditions (*pratyaya*)?
If it does not follow conditions, how can the wondrousness of this mind be manifested? Answer: This mind neither follows nor does not follow;
it follows yet does not follow, is neither following nor non-following, and is neither non-following nor following. It is simply attained through detachment.
Cut off from the four propositions and beyond the hundred negations, when the mouth wishes to speak, words fail; when the mind seeks to contemplate, thought vanishes.
A single raised eyebrow is ten thousand miles of white clouds; a blink of an eye is a hawk soaring over Silla. Even when the World-Honored One arrives here, there is no place to set down his words.
Yet, having no choice but to speak, he says: "Neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing."

The preceding subtraction of characters serves merely as a commentary; one must know that these four lines of scripture truly elucidate the essential nature of one's own mind in this way—how could one not strive toward this?

Because this mind of one's own is fundamentally devoid of the arising-phase of ignorance, fundamentally devoid of the abiding-phase of ignorance, fundamentally devoid of the differentiation-phase of ignorance, and fundamentally devoid of the cessation-phase of ignorance, it is said to be "unborn."
It is not extinguished; by virtue of being neither born nor extinguished, it abides in a state of subtle difference. Furthermore, this self-mind is fundamentally without greed, anger, or delusion;

fundamentally without killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct; fundamentally without the five desires, birth, or death; fundamentally without the three realms or the six paths of existence; fundamentally without false views or external paths;
and fundamentally without precepts, concentration, or wisdom, nor without the six perfections or the myriad practices. It is fundamentally nothing at all.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas originally lack [the status of] Buddhas and bodhisattvas;
taken as a whole, all defiled dharmas are unobtainable and all pure dharmas are unobtainable—therefore it is said they are "neither defiled nor pure.
Nevertheless, this mind can, according to circumstances and without fixed direction, manifest the four realms of the noble ones and manifest the six realms of ordinary beings; yet, this mind...

In the realm of the four noble ones, not a single hair’s breadth is added; in the realm of the six classes of ordinary beings, not a single hair’s breadth is subtracted. It is truly equal and impartial, without high or low; therefore, it is called "neither increasing nor decreasing. Question: This sutra takes the mind as its primary subject; should it not take the mind as its central tenet? Why then does it take contemplative observation (*guanzhao*) as its central tenet? Answer: There are two meanings to this. First, although the mind is the source of all dharmas, if one does not contemplate it, one will not realize its true nature. Second, the mind is inherently pure, yet it is obscured by adventitious afflictions; only through contemplative observation can these afflictions be eliminated and the original purity be restored. Therefore, while the mind is the essence, contemplative observation is the method for realizing that essence. Thus, it is said that the mind is the substance and contemplative observation is the function. Since the function is the means to realize the substance, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Furthermore, the mind is difficult to perceive and easy to err in; if one does not apply contemplative observation, one will fail to see its reality. For this reason, the sutra emphasizes contemplative observation as the primary practice. Finally, the mind is the root of birth and death, while contemplative observation is the gate to nirvana. To sever the cycle of birth and death and attain the fruit of liberation, one must rely on contemplative observation. Therefore, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. These are the two reasons why, although the mind is the subject, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Furthermore, the mind is like a mirror; if one does not polish it with the cloth of contemplative observation, its brightness will not manifest. Only through the application of contemplative observation can the mirror of the mind be polished until it reflects all things clearly. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Moreover, the mind is like water; if one does not stir it with the hand of contemplative observation, its clarity will not emerge. Only through the application of contemplative observation can the water of the mind be stirred until it becomes clear and still. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Furthermore, the mind is like gold; if one does not refine it with the fire of contemplative observation, its brilliance will not appear. Only through the application of contemplative observation can the gold of the mind be refined until its luster shines forth. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Moreover, the mind is like a seed; if one does not provide the moisture of contemplative observation, it will not sprout. Only through the application of contemplative observation can the seed of the mind be moistened until it germinates and grows. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Furthermore, the mind is like a field; if one does not sow the seeds of contemplative observation, there will be no harvest. Only through the application of contemplative observation can the field of the mind be cultivated until the fruit of enlightenment is attained. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Finally, the mind is like a king; if one does not employ the ministers of contemplative observation, the kingdom will not be governed. Only through the application of contemplative observation can the king of the mind exercise its sovereign power. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. These are the various reasons why, although the mind is the subject, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Furthermore, the mind is the master of all dharmas, yet it is difficult to control. Contemplative observation is the whip of wisdom; only when the whip of contemplative observation is applied can the mind be brought under control. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Moreover, the mind is the source of all suffering, yet it is difficult to transform. Contemplative observation is the medicine of liberation; only when the medicine of contemplative observation is taken can the mind be transformed. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Furthermore, the mind is the root of all phenomena, yet it is difficult to penetrate. Contemplative observation is the sword of insight; only when the sword of contemplative observation is drawn can the root of the mind be severed. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Moreover, the mind is the foundation of all virtues, yet it is difficult to stabilize. Contemplative observation is the pillar of stability; only when the pillar of contemplative observation is erected can the foundation of the mind be made firm. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Finally, the mind is the vessel of the Dharma, yet it is difficult to purify. Contemplative observation is the cleansing agent; only when the cleansing agent of contemplative observation is applied can the vessel of the mind be purified. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. These are the various reasons why, although the mind is the subject, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Furthermore, the mind is the origin of all delusions, yet it is difficult to dispel. Contemplative observation is the light of wisdom; only when the light of contemplative observation shines can the darkness of delusion be dispelled. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Moreover, the mind is the treasury of the Tathāgata, yet it is difficult to open. Contemplative observation is the key; only when the key of contemplative observation is used can the treasury of the mind be opened. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Furthermore, the mind is the path to Buddhahood, yet it is difficult to traverse. Contemplative observation is the guide; only when the guide of contemplative observation leads the way can the path of the mind be traversed. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Moreover, the mind is the ground of liberation, yet it is difficult to ascend. Contemplative observation is the ladder; only when the ladder of contemplative observation is climbed can the ground of liberation be reached. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Finally, the mind is the source of all Buddhas, yet it is difficult to realize. Contemplative observation is the realization; only when the realization of contemplative observation is attained can the source of the mind be realized. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. These are the various reasons why, although the mind is the subject, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Furthermore, the mind is the essence of all dharmas, yet it is difficult to perceive. Contemplative observation is the perception; only when the perception of contemplative observation is achieved can the essence of the mind be perceived. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Moreover, the mind is the body of the Dharma, yet it is difficult to manifest. Contemplative observation is the manifestation; only when the manifestation of contemplative observation occurs can the body of the mind be manifested. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Furthermore, the mind is the power of the Buddha, yet it is difficult to exert. Contemplative observation is the exertion; only when the exertion of contemplative observation is applied can the power of the mind be exerted. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Moreover, the mind is the wisdom of the Tathāgata, yet it is difficult to awaken to. Contemplative observation is the awakening; only when the awakening of contemplative observation is attained can the wisdom of the mind be awakened to. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Finally, the mind is the nature of reality, yet it is difficult to enter. Contemplative observation is the entry; only when the entry of contemplative observation is made can the nature of the mind be entered. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. These are the various reasons why, although the mind is the subject, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Furthermore, the mind is the source of all teachings, yet it is difficult to understand. Contemplative observation is the understanding; only when the understanding of contemplative observation is reached can the source of the mind be understood. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Moreover, the mind is the root of all practices, yet it is difficult to cultivate. Contemplative observation is the cultivation; only when the cultivation of contemplative observation is practiced can the root of the mind be cultivated. For this reason, the sutra takes contemplative observation as its central tenet. Furthermore, the mind is the foundation of all merits, yet it is difficult to accumulate. Contemplative observation is the accumulation; only when the accumulation of contemplative observation is performed can the foundation of the mind be accumulated. Regarding the first point, "not taking the mind as the primary principle": I follow the ancients and do not dare to alter it arbitrarily, for the ancients judged that contemplation and illumination (*guan-zhao*) constitute the primary principle.
However, according to my own view, I take the true mark (*shixiang*) as the essence, the self-mind as the primary principle, and contemplation and illumination as the function;
I take the *amṛta* (clarified butter) as the characteristic of the teaching. As for the phrase "the mind-principle, illumination, and function," let us set that aside for now.
Why is the teaching of Prajñāpāramitā called "the cream of ghee" (*amṛta*)? If it is indeed the cream of ghee, it should reside in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
why then is it designated as Prajñā? The answer is: in terms of time, it is Prajñā; in terms of the flavor of the teaching, it is the cream of ghee.

This is because, among the five periods [of the Buddha’s teaching], there exists the "indeterminate teaching. Furthermore, this Mind-essence is the source of all dharmas and the sovereign of all sūtras.

That which is called "mind" is the fundamental basis of all dhāraṇīs and the vast source of all phenomena. Therefore, I, your humble servant, have judged it to be the essence of *amṛta* (clarified butter).
I merely submit this for the esteemed judgment of those of lofty intelligence; what do you think? Question:
Since the mind is thus manifest and supreme, why does the World-Honored One here not speak of the mind but speaks only of emptiness? What is the meaning of this? Answer: The World-Honored One—

With this intention, [the Master] considered that because all sentient beings falsely identify the "bright and numinous" as their own mind, they either cling to it as being inside, outside, or within the six sense organs; thus, by forcibly asserting a sovereign self, they are truly attached to partiality and error.
Now, if one were to speak directly of "mind," there is a fear that people would instead take their own attachments and project them onto this wondrous mind.
What further benefit would there be in this deluded mind? Only by examining the concluding summary in the subsequent text can one see the subtlety of its intent.
Therefore, this section merely uses empty words to awaken those who encounter it, requiring each person to realize it for themselves;

it speaks of knowing the ultimate destination beyond all things, meaning that one must first recognize the fundamental principle. Thus, when the compiler of the sutra titles this with "Mind" and "Eye," we further know the Buddha’s...

This subtle intention—should it not be relied upon? A question is raised: regarding the phrase "the empty nature of all dharmas" (*sarva-dharma-śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*) in the text, does the term *sarva* (all) refer only to the two [categories] of the aggregates (*skandha*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as being unobtainable? The answer is: There are two meanings.
First, because there are five aggregates and the emptiness manifested by them, they are collectively referred to as "all. Second, the term "all" is used by analogy with the aggregates and emptiness.
Because the various faculties and bodies, as well as the diverse realms of the vessel-world, can all be mutually inferred, they are said to be "all manifested downward.
Therefore, within emptiness, there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; there are no eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, or mind; and there is no form.
There is no realm of sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena; nor is there the realm of the eye, up to and including the realm of consciousness.

This demonstrates that [these factors] are ungraspable by means of the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six sense organs (*indriya*), the six sense objects (*viṣaya*), and the twelve bases (*āyatana*).

Thus, having first investigated the emptiness of the aggregates and dependent origination, one subsequently realizes the single essence of one's own mind; yet this realization of the mind ultimately arises from conditions.
Because it arises and only then arrives, I now further clarify that all phenomena arise through conditions;

by finally concluding that they return to one's own mind, one perceives the subtle intent behind both the preceding and succeeding sections. For if, at the outset, one does not analyze the emptiness of the aggregates, ordinary beings cannot avoid the error of false attachment;
therefore, one must first analyze the emptiness of the aggregates. Next, if one does not bring them back to one's own mind, [the practice remains incomplete].
Fearing that the Prajñā might be perceived as merely empty, appearing to possess a subtle state that does not engage with conditions,

and that Śrāvakas would consequently remain settled upon the bed of non-action (asaṃskṛta) without even perceiving it, one must next necessarily return to one's own mind to finally see its perfect subtlety.
If the nature of dependent origination were not extensively revealed herein, there would be a fear that the myriad dharmas would remain unexhausted.
Because of these doubts, one must extensively reveal the myriad dharmas before seeing through to the bottom and becoming free of doubt;

it is only upon concluding by returning to the self-mind at the end that the matter becomes ultimately complete and perfect. For this reason, the reasons why the meaning of the preceding and following passages has varying degrees of concealment and manifestation lies precisely here.
Within this, the extensive revelation of dependent origination first concerns the five aggregates and the six sense faculties.
Regarding the six objects, twelve bases, and eighteen elements: the five aggregates herein are identical to those previously analyzed;
there is no need for a further explanation. One might ask: since the five aggregates have already been fully analyzed, why are they presented again?

The answer is that this merely borrows the previous meaning to serve as an analogy for what follows; therefore, they are not explained anew. As for what are called the six sense organs (*indriya*): the eye organ is like a reed.
The clusters of blossoms merely rush toward form; yet this root of the eye is fundamentally non-existent.

This is because, within the wondrous perfection, the two objects of light and darkness adhere to the profound stillness to give rise to seeing. The essence of seeing becomes afflicted by form, and through its attachment to form, it forms a root.
Thus one knows that the eye-root, apart from its deluded seeing and deluded objects, is fundamentally non-existent. Therefore, this root is—

This is because dependent origination can no longer be apprehended; the ear-organ is like a newly rolled leaf that rushes toward sound. Furthermore, this ear-organ originally has no existence of its own;
it arises from the two objects of motion and stillness, which, within the wondrously perfect [nature], cause the clarity to become adhered and give rise to hearing.
When the rolling of hearing reflects the essence and the rolling of sound constitutes the organ, one knows that the ear-organ is nothing but deluded hearing and deluded sound.
This root is fundamentally non-existent; thus, this root is simply dependent origination and can no longer be apprehended.
The nose-root is like a pair of hanging melons, rushing toward fragrance alone. Furthermore, this nose-root is fundamentally non-existent;

it arises because the two objects—permeability and obstruction—within the wondrous perfection cause turbidity to adhere to the profound stillness, giving rise to smelling. The essence of smelling reflects fragrance and receives fragrance, thereby forming [the faculty].
As for the faculty of smell, one knows that its false smelling and false fragrances are fundamentally non-existent;
thus, this faculty is simply dependent origination and can no longer be apprehended. The faculty of taste is like a crescent moon, rushing toward flavors;
yet this faculty of taste is fundamentally non-existent, for it arises from the two objects of tranquility and change adhering to the profound stillness within the wondrous perfection.
When the sense of taste repeatedly encounters the essence of calamitous flavors and the flavor of constriction, it forms a root;

yet one knows that this root is eliminated when its tranquil transformations and deluded tastes are fundamentally non-existent. Thus, this root is simply dependent origination and can no longer be apprehended.
The body-root is like the head of a waist-drum, rushing only toward contact; moreover, this body-root is fundamentally non-existent, for it arises from detachment.

When the two objects are joined within the wondrous perfection, they adhere to the profound stillness to give rise to awareness; the essence of awareness reflects the contact, and by seizing upon that contact, the faculty is formed.
Thus one knows that this faculty, apart from its false awareness of joining and separating, fundamentally has no existence.

Therefore, this faculty is a dependent origination and can no longer be grasped as a self-entity. As for the mental faculty, it is like seeing in a dark chamber; it merely rushes toward phenomena. Furthermore, this—
The fundamental non-existence of the mind-organ arises because the two objects of arising and ceasing adhere to the wondrous perfection, causing the clarity of stillness to give rise to cognition;

this cognitive essence reflects phenomena and grasps them to form the organ. Thus, one should know that this organ, when stripped of its arising and ceasing, is fundamentally non-existent as a false cognition.
Therefore, this organ is merely a dependent origination and can no longer be apprehended. As for what is called "form":

Although there are many kinds of sensory objects (*viṣaya*), they ultimately converge upon a single meaning. For instance, when the Buddha asked Ānanda, "Observe the Jeta Grove forest and the various springs and ponds;
these are the sensory objects of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*)," the text extensively elaborates upon this, which cannot be cited in its entirety here.
Now, taking a brief excerpt, I shall provide my own commentary; subsequent examples shall follow this pattern. Furthermore, these sensory objects of form originally do not exist at all, for...
It exists through the differentiation of the eye-faculty and eye-consciousness; were it not for this eye-faculty and eye-consciousness, these visual objects would no longer exist.
Furthermore, these visual objects arise solely from conditions.
As for the auditory objects, although they are of many kinds, they ultimately have but one meaning. For instance, as the Buddha asked Ānanda: "Listen again to this Śītavana grove."
When the meal is prepared, the drum is struck and the assembly gathers; the bell is then tolled—this is the auditory object (*śabda-viṣaya*). Yet this auditory object, too, does not truly exist.

It arises through the differentiation of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) and the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*). If there were no faculty and consciousness, from where could sound be obtained?
Thus one knows that the auditory object has no further existence. Furthermore, this auditory object also arises from conditions (*pratyaya*); as it is said:
Although the objects of the sense of smell (*gandha-viṣaya*) are of many kinds, they ultimately resolve into a single principle. For example, as the Buddha told Ānanda:
"You again smell this sandalwood in the incense burner; this is the object of smell. Furthermore, this object of smell originally does not exist;

it arises only through the discrimination of the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) and the olfactory consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*). If there were no discrimination, the fragrance could not be apprehended. Thus one should know.
The sensory object of fragrance arises solely from conditions; as for the sensory object of taste, it is likewise manifold. For instance, as the World-Honored One told Ānanda:
"When you constantly carry your alms bowl among the assembly at the two meal times, you may encounter ghee, curd, or clarified butter, which are called superior flavors.
This is the sensory object of taste, which exists through the faculty and consciousness, just as in the previous example. As for the sensory object of touch...
As the World-Honored One told Ānanda: "When you regularly rub your head with your hand in the early morning, this is the sense-object of touch (*spraṣṭavya-dhātu*);
it arises from the faculty and consciousness, just as in the previous examples. As for the sense-object of mental phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*), as the World-Honored One said:

'That which is constantly contemplated by your mind—the three natures of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—this constitutes the principle of mental phenomena (*dharma*); this is the sense-object of mental phenomena.'"
There are no further precedents for this. As for what is called a "realm" (*dhātu*), the Sanskrit term *dhātu* translates here as "realm.

It carries the sense of "cause," because the three—sense organ, object, and consciousness—act as causes for one another. Furthermore, it carries the sense of "lineage" (*gotra*), because the three—organ, object, and consciousness—each constitute a distinct lineage.
Moreover, since there are six distinct lineages, such as the eye and so forth, these eighteen realms likewise do not exist.

Generally speaking, the term "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to the three factors of sense organ, object, and consciousness. Since one sense organ has three [corresponding] objects and three [corresponding] consciousnesses, there are eighteen.
These eighteen, when investigated, possess no intrinsic substance; for the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses themselves lack intrinsic substance.

If these three lack existence, from what could a "realm" be established? Thus, these eighteen realms are also merely dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); this is how they should be understood.

The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* makes it easy for people to understand; however, I have not recorded its full text but have instead selected specific phrases and meanings, hoping that by tasting a single morsel one may come to know the entire cauldron.
Someone might say, "This [text] differs from the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*. I reply that they are in fact identical;
it is simply that while the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* employs various methods of logical refutation, this text directly conveys the meaning of the text itself. Although there are differences...
"Though their expressions differ, their essential meaning is truly one. Question: "In this context, it would suffice to speak directly and conclude immediately;

why is it necessary to investigate through the principle of dependent origination? Answer: "If one does not investigate dependent origination, by what means could ordinary people attain understanding?
It must necessarily be so. For instance, even Ānanda, who was foremost among those of great learning,"
Yet, how much more so for people like us, who must investigate through various methods of debate!
There is neither ignorance nor the exhaustion of ignorance, and so on, up to neither old age and death nor the exhaustion of old age and death.
This reveals that the path of the Pratyekabuddha, which consists of the twelve links of dependent origination, is itself dependently arisen.
Furthermore, these twelve links of dependent origination possess both arising and cessation. Regarding "arising":

it is because within the true nature (*tathatā*), a single thought-moment of non-awakening causes the true nature to be obscured; this is called ignorance (*avidyā*). Due to this lack of clarity, one falsely...
When there is movement, it is called "volitional formation" (*saṃskāra*); because of this movement, there is discrimination, which is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*);
because of this discrimination, there is entry into the womb and the stages of the embryo—*kalala*, *arbuda*, *peśī*, and *ghana*—which is called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*);
because of name-and-form, the six sense faculties gradually develop, which is called the "six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*); and because of the six sense bases, [there arises contact].
Contacting the objects of the six sense-fields is called "contact" (*sparśa*).

Because there is contact, one experiences the three types of objects—those that are disagreeable, agreeable, or neutral—which is called "feeling" (*vedanā*). Because there is feeling, one gives rise to craving:

craving for disagreeable objects leads to constant avoidance; craving for agreeable objects leads to constant pursuit; and regarding neutral objects, before craving arises, one remains detached, but once it has arisen, one becomes attached.
When there is the long-term union of craving, it is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*); because there is the grasping due to craving, it is called "grasping" (*upādāna*);
because there is grasping, there is the connection with the fruits of karma, which is called "becoming" (*bhava*);

because there are the fruits of karma, they belong to sentient beings, which is called "birth" (*jāti*); because there is birth, there is aging and death, which is called "aging and death" (*jarāmaraṇa*). These [constitute] the whole.
Because the twelve factors that initiate existence serve as causes and the twelve auxiliary factors serve as conditions, they are called "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, these twelve links of dependent origination pertain to the three periods of time: ignorance conditions volitional formations—these two past factors are the cause;
consciousness conditions name-and-form, and name-and-form conditions the six sense bases, continuing down to contact conditioning feeling—these five present factors are the fruit.
When there is the formative action of ignorance, it necessarily brings about such a fruit;

with craving as the condition for grasping, and grasping as the condition for becoming—these two present factors being causes because they must produce the fruit of retribution, and because there must first be such causal afflictions to give rise to the two future factors of old age and death as their conditions and fruits—since there are these present causes, they necessarily bring about future fruits. Thus it is.
The cycle of the three periods of time, with its constant emergence and submergence, is truly something to be weary of and renounce.

Therefore, when those seeking the state of a Pratyekabuddha hear of these twelve links of dependent origination, they immediately seek renunciation and cultivate contemplative practice in order to sever and extinguish them.
It is just as when cutting down a tree: one must first strike at the root; once the root is severed, the branches and leaves will certainly no longer remain. Now...
The desire to extinguish these twelve links of dependent origination is likewise so: if one wishes to extinguish the root, one must first extinguish ignorance (*avidyā*).
If ignorance is extinguished, the twelve links of dependent origination will likewise cease to exist. Therefore it is said: "With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) cease;
... and so on, until old age and death also cease. This is what is meant by the exhaustion of ignorance, and [the cessation of] old age and death as well.
When the causes and conditions are exhausted and have ceased, one enters *nirvāṇa with remainder*; this is the path of the *pratyekabuddha*.
However, this path of the *pratyekabuddha* is in truth also devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

For the causes and conditions of arising are manifested through their cessation, and the causes and conditions of cessation are manifested through arising. Since these causes mutually manifest one another and both lack substantial essence, [the path is without self-nature].
The path of the Pratyekabuddha is truly because both [subject and object] are unattainable through dependent origination; thus it is said:
"there is no ignorance, up to and including no extinction of ignorance," and so forth. There is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; there is no wisdom, nor is there any attainment.
This reveals that the paths of both the śrāvakas and the bodhisattvas regarding the Four Noble Truths are also dependent origination.

Furthermore, among the Four Noble Truths, suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) belong to the causal relationship of the mundane world, while cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) belong to the causal relationship of the supramundane. Regarding the mundane causal relationship:
the origin is the nature of being summoned and experienced, and suffering is the nature of oppression; it is through greed, hatred, and delusion that one summons and experiences retribution.
Karma thus brings about oppression; this nature of oppression does not transcend the eight types of suffering.

These eight sufferings involve immeasurable perils and calamities that are truly loathsome. Because the śrāvakas recognize these sufferings, they cultivate the path of morality, concentration, and wisdom to enter the quiescent nirvāṇa.
This is what is meant by abandoning worldly causes and effects to cultivate the supramundane.
The same applies to cause and effect; these two types of cause and effect likewise lack any substantial nature, as illustrated by the path of the pratyekabuddha.

Furthermore, the path of the bodhisattva is vast and immeasurable: in its entirety it comprises the ten thousand practices (*sāhasra-caryā*), in brief it consists of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), and when condensed, it is subsumed under the two terms "wisdom" (*jñāna*) and "attainment" (*prāpti*).
Because it possesses wisdom, it brings about both self-benefit and the benefit of others.

It is also said that [the fruit] is attained; however, the path of the Bodhisattva likewise arises from conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*). If there were no arising from conditions, how could practice be applied?
Thus we know that the path of the Bodhisattva cannot be attained apart from conditions, as in the previous examples.

Furthermore, the term "wisdom" (*jñāna*) pertains to the Bodhisattva, while the term "attainment" (*prāpti*) pertains to the Buddhas; this is because the Bodhisattva belongs to the stage of the cause (*hetu*).
Because of wisdom, all Buddhas are subsumed under the attainment of the fruit;
yet, since there is no distinction between mind, Buddha, and sentient beings, one knows that the Buddhas, too, are dependently originated and ungraspable.

One must understand that the infinite myriad dharmas do not transcend the two realms of the holy and the ordinary, which encompass them exhaustively. Therefore, although this is now presented in four sections through words to clarify it...
Because the investigation of dependent origination is truly immeasurable, it is said that "the extensive manifestation of dependent origination" can be known;
having thus completed the exposition of arising, the text below concludes by returning to the core point:
because there is nothing to be apprehended, the Bodhisattva, relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, has a mind free from hindrance.
Because there is no obstruction, there is no fear; being far removed from inverted thoughts and delusions, one attains ultimate Nirvana.

This is what is meant by "returning to one's own mind. For the preceding section extensively revealed that dependent origination is itself emptiness of nature, and that Prajñā-pāramitā is non-apprehension;
therefore it says, "because of non-apprehension. Furthermore, the word "therefore" (故) here refers to—
The phrase "there is a bond" (*saṃyojana*) clarifies the intended meaning; the character "hence" (*gù*) below follows this pattern.

Because the Bodhisattva relies on this prajñā of the emptiness of nature to perfectly realize their own mind, leaving nothing remaining, it is designated as: "Relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, the mind is without hindrance.
Furthermore, this mind does not abide for even a single moment; like a great mass of fire, not even a hair’s breadth remains.
The flash of lightning admits no room for deliberation; dwelling in existence is ruined by existence, and dwelling in emptiness is defeated by emptiness.
One must simply attain the severance of thought and the cessation of the sphere of mental activity (*cittagocara*), such that not a single thing confronts the mind to act as an obstacle.
If the nature of the mind and its phenomena is thus supreme, why fear it and not eliminate it? Why do you not distance yourself from such delusions? What is this dream?
If one’s perceptions can be disturbed, how could *nirvāṇa* be attainable? Therefore, it is stated: "Because there are no hindrances, there is no fear;
far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, one reaches ultimate *nirvāṇa*. Is this not a direct discourse as well? Furthermore, this fear originally has no substantial essence;
it arises only because people do not fully comprehend all phenomena (*dharmas*) and thus give rise to alarm and dread.
Out of fear and dread, one harbors terrors, which give rise to various dreams and unreal, false attachments regarding *nirvāṇa*.
Yet, how could such a *nirvāṇa* actually be attained? All of this is merely the dharma of ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*).

Because ordinary people do not understand that all phenomena are but mind-only, they give rise to delusions and create karma; thus, they may create the worlds of the hells and the three miserable paths.

Whether one practices the supramundane dharmas of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, or even seeks to attain the dharma of Great Nirvāṇa, all of these arise solely from the delusions and terrors produced by the mind.
When examined through correct reasoning, they are all like dreams—illusory arisings and illusory vanishings that possess no substantial reality.
They are like the phantom bow and arrow seen in a cup of water, which cause false delusions and fear.
"Is fear not likewise empty and deceptive? Now this Bodhisattva has realized and witnessed that such dreams and illusions within his own mind are entirely non-existent.
[The interlocutor] asked: "If one believes that dreams and illusions do not exist, why then would Nirvana also be non-existent?

If it does not exist, where could the Bodhisattva reach ultimate realization? [The Master] replied: "This is yet another instance of failing to understand one's own mind, leading you to harbor such doubts."
If one realizes one's own mind, even the single word "Buddha" is but a name and a sign; how much more so, then, is *nirvāṇa*?
When the entirety of empty space and the pervasive dharma-realm are a single,浑浑 (hún hún) whole of the self, how could there be room for names and signs within it?
Have you not seen the scholar Zhang Zhuo, who was but a worldly man, yet upon awakening to his own mind, immediately declared: "Luminous and quiescently illuminating"?
Throughout the sands of the Ganges, ordinary beings and sages, all sentient creatures, share one family. When not a single thought arises, the entire reality is fully revealed;

as soon as the six sense-faculties stir, they are shrouded by clouds. To sever deluded thoughts is to increase the illness once more; to seek toward True Suchness (Tathatā) is likewise a form of deviation.
Flowing along with worldly conditions without hindrance, nirvana and birth-and-death are equal to flowers in the sky. Relying on this faith, proceed of your own accord.
This is indeed so.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This phrase clarifies that all Buddhas likewise realize their own minds through the emptiness of the nature of *prajñā*.
Although "Anuttara" is a designation for the fruit [of Buddhahood], it is in fact another name for one's own mind.
